newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala army moves on rebel military police.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala army moves on rebel military police.

text.p: The Guatemalan army deployed troops and tanks on Saturday night around a compound held by rebellious military police in a four-day dispute over peacetime changes in the armed forces, witnesses said.

Military policemen outside their fortified compound told a Reuters photographer that three tanks drove by the compound and soldiers shot at them and that they shot back. They said they would fight back if the army moved against them.
The military police reported no injuries but said soldiers had taken up positions around the compound in a residential district of the capital.
The confrontation marks an escalation in the military police protest which has been the first sign of military discontent over terms of a peace accord signed in December.
The military police took over their own headquarters on Wednesday night demanding guarantees of severance pay when the government dissolves their entire 4,000-member unit later this year.
Military police have refused to report to work guarding banks and businesses in the capital during the protest.
According to reports by Radio Sonora the army has set up a command centre near the compound and blocked off streets in the area. The army also placed ambulances nearby.
One of three generals who tried earlier on Saturday to negotiate with the military police and who was then blocked from leaving the compound remained hostage on Saturday night.
Until Saturday's army movements, the government played down the rebellion. Presidential spokesman Ricardo de la Torre called the revolt a "labor dispute."
Drastic army reductions are part of terms in the peace treaty signed Dec. 29 between the government and leftist rebels the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit, which ended 36 years of civil war.
The conflict claimed an estimated 140,000 lives in civilian casualties.
The army has played a pivotal and at times, a brutal role in political life for much of Guatemala's recent history.

Police complain the guerrillas of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit had won a better deal in the peace accords than they did. International aid will provide job training and housing assistance for ex-rebels.
